messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mr. Tran, a 69-year-old South Eastern Asian widower and nanny, has been struggling with the aftermath of his grandson’s life-threatening illness several years ago. This event, which occurred when Mr. Tran was taking care of his young grandson while the parents were away on business, left him feeling profoundly changed and unable to make sense of what happened. The night started like any other until a sudden high fever turned into severe convulsions that sent both of them rushing to the emergency room. The harrowing moments in the ER—seeing his grandson’s body thrashing uncontrollably and then slipping into unconsciousness—felt more real than anything Mr. Tran had experienced before. Now, these memories feel like they are happening all over again, as if the trauma was a recent event rather than something that happened years ago. Mr. Tran has come to believe that his actions during this crisis were what kept his grandson alive, and yet he feels unrecognizable to himself—a person who once was calm and steady but is now plagued by an ever-present fear of making mistakes again. This belief has deepened his sense of distrust towards others; he feels people are not what they seem, and this fuels a constant vigilance that makes it difficult for him to relax. This heightened state of alertness manifests in how Mr. Tran interacts with the world around him. He tries hard not to think about the trauma but finds himself constantly seeking distractions, keeping his mind occupied all the time. When he does allow himself to think about what happened, those memories feel overwhelmingly vivid and real, as if they are happening again right now. This recurrent intensity makes it challenging for Mr. Tran to maintain a coherent story of the event; he cannot even tell a clear account of what happened to himself. Mr. Tran’s fear that his experiences have permanently changed him for the worse has led him to avoid seeking medical or psychological help, as he believes there is no point in doing so. Instead, he relies on suppressing thoughts and distracting himself with other tasks. This avoidance, however, only deepens his negative appraisals. He finds it increasingly difficult to trust others and is convinced that any attempt to seek help will only remind him of the trauma. The intense memories also exacerbate his maladaptive strategies. Whenever Mr. Tran thinks about seeking medical care, the vividness of those traumatic moments immediately surfaces, making such actions seem impossible. This cycle leaves him feeling trapped in a perpetual state of fear and self-doubt. Mr. Tran’s daily life as a nanny has become increasingly strained due to these challenges. He avoids taking on tasks that might trigger memories of his grandson’s illness, leading to fewer hours at work and strained relationships with the families he cares for. Despite these consequences, Mr. Tran is reluctant to address his fears directly because he believes that doing so will only reinforce his belief in a permanently damaged self. What finally brought Mr. Tran to seek help was the realization that his grandson’s illness had profoundly affected not just him but also those around him. He is most afraid of losing control again, of being unable to protect someone he loves. At the same time, he hopes for a way to find peace and regain some sense of who he used to be. Mr. Tran understands that addressing these fears will require facing them head-on, but he is determined to do so in order to reclaim his life and find a path forward.
